# Block 1: AI-assisted R programming {.unnumbered} ## Prerequisites You need a GitHub account, a working IDE (RStudio, Positron, or VS Code), and basic Git and GitHub fluency at the level of cloning a repository, making a branch, opening a pull request, and merging. Block 9 also assumes a working knowledge of `renv` and `testthat`, both covered in earlier sessions. The workshop's main tool is **Claude Code**, Anthropic's agent that runs in a terminal. You need a Claude Pro or Max subscription, a Claude for Teams or Enterprise seat, or a Claude Console account billed per request. Installing it and running the checks in [Setting up Claude Code](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd) is **pre-work**: do it before the day. If you prefer to work inside RStudio or Positron, **Posit Assistant** is supported as an alternative. It runs on a Posit AI subscription or on a provider key you supply, and each page notes where it differs from Claude Code. **GitHub Copilot** is needed only for inline completion in Block 2, for which Copilot Free is enough, and for the optional cloud-agent material in some *Going further* sections, which needs a paid plan. Check the [Copilot plans page](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/get-started/plans) for what is currently available. Whichever tools you use, check that your institution permits them, and if you will use them near research data, that your ethics approval and data agreements allow it. Block 4 covers this in detail. ## Learning outcomes By the end of the workshop, you will be able to: 1. Articulate what a large language model is, and explain what choosing between underlying models materially affects. 2. Use inline completion in your chosen IDE, and identify what context the tool can and cannot see. 3. Use AI assistance to debug code you have written, and recognise the cases in which AI is most and least useful for debugging. 4. Explain what an assistant can see and do, identify every route by which your data leave your machine, and choose an appropriate level of autonomy for a task. 5. Write and test an `AGENTS.md` instruction file and a skill, and explain why both are requests to the model rather than guarantees. 6. Test a permission rule that protects raw data, find a route around it, and detect any change with git. 7. Clean data with an agent against a codebook you own, and check the result with validation rules and an audit of every change. 8. Use AI as a code reviewer and grade its findings against a known answer key. 9. Have an agent functionalise a script step under a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct., keeping the reference in your own hands, and explain why an unchanged result is not necessarily a correct one. 10. Check an AI translation of analysis code for equivalence, report results without typed numbers, and leave with a documented repository: a README drafted only from verifiable inputs, and a log of your AI use. ## The day at a glance | Time | Session | |---|---| | 09:00 | Block 1: AI-assisted R programming (15 min) | | 09:15 | Blocks 2–3: Inline completions; Debugging with AI (45 min) | | 10:00 | Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy (33 min) | | 10:33 | Break | | 10:48 | Block 5: Instructions and skills (45 min) | | 11:33 | Block 6: Enforced controls (30 min) | | 12:03 | Lunch | | 13:03 | Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI (54 min) | | 13:57 | Block 8: AI-assisted code review (40 min) | | 14:37 | Break | | 14:52 | Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged (38 min) | | 15:30 | Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results (30 min) | | 16:00 | Close | Each block from Block 2 onwards ends with a *Going further* section that is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ## Materials Participants will work with a synthetic biological dataset (`voles_metabolism.csv`) and a workshop template repository that they fork before the day (its layout is in [Your workshop repository](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#your-workshop-repository)). The template uses `renv` for project-local packages, so after forking and opening the project, run `renv::restore()` once as part of the pre-work. Block 7 uses a copy of the voles data with errors planted in it, which your instructor supplies, and Block 8 uses the project folder from that you reviewed by hand on Day 2. ## A note on platform variation - **Claude Code** runs in a terminal: the Terminal tab in RStudio, the integrated terminal in Positron or VS Code, or your system terminal. It works alongside any IDE, and it acts on the project folder you start it from. The main text of every block uses it. - **Posit Assistant** is the alternative: the in-IDE chat and agent in RStudio and Positron, which can see your live R session as well as your project files. See [What's new in Posit AI](https://docs.posit.co/posit-ai/whats-new/). Where it differs from Claude Code, a collapsed *Using Posit Assistant* box says how. - **GitHub Copilot** provides the inline completions in Block 2, in all three IDEs. **Verification is the workshop's only non-negotiable.** AI tools generate plausible code quickly. They do not guarantee correctness, and they do not relieve you of responsibility for what your code does. Every exercise in this workshop ends with a verification step. Treat that step as the most important part of the exercise. ## The thread through the day: Check · Reproduce · Record Every block applies the same three habits to a different task, and each block ends with a short box saying what it added to each: - **Check.** Treat everything an AI produces as a claim, and verify it with something independent of the AI: the data, a test, a reference you hold, `git diff`, or your own knowledge of the biology. - **Reproduce.** Make sure the result does not depend on the session it came from. The code runs from a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work, such as the one Rscript starts. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., the package versions are the ones in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment. (`renv.lock`), and nothing was installed or changed that you did not see. Day 1 introduced `renv`; Day 4 checks that an agent has kept to it. - **Record.** Leave the evidence a reader needs: a codebook, a log of every change to the data, numbers computed in code rather than typed, and a log of your AI use. On Day 2 you saw what a reviewable project needs ([TADA! and the README](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-fix), and [the SORTEE checklist](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-sortee)); Day 4 shows how AI can help produce that record without inventing any of it. By the end of the day your workshop repository holds that record. Each block adds to it, and Block 10 draws it together in a README: ::::::: {.dia .dia-flow role="figure" aria-label="Files that accumulate in your workshop repository through the day: Block 4 adds the AI-use log; Block 5 adds AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and a skill; Block 6 tests the shipped settings file; Block 7 adds the codebook and cleaning and exclusion logs; Block 9 adds the reference and tests; Block 10 adds a README that draws on all of them."} ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 4** `docs/ai-log.md` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 5** `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, a skill ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 6** `settings.json` in `.claude/`, read and tested ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 7** codebook, cleaning and exclusion logs ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 9** reference and tests ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} **Block 10** `README.md`, drawing on all of them ::: ::: {.dia-caption} Check · Reproduce · Record: what your repository holds by 16:00. ::: ::::::: **Your AI-use log.** From Block 4 onwards you will add one line to `docs/ai-log.md` in your workshop repository after each block in which an agent does work. This AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. is written by you, not by the agent. Each line has this form: ``` date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed ``` Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use. A log written at the time is easier and more accurate than one reconstructed later, and in Block 10 it becomes the AI declaration in your README. ## Claude Code quick reference {#cc-quick-reference} Keep this open during the day. All of these are typed in the terminal where Claude Code is running. | To... | Do this | |---|---| | Start Claude Code in your workshop repository | `cd` to the repository's root folder, then `claude` | | Start in read-only planning mode | `claude --permission-mode plan` | | Change how much it may do without asking | `Shift+Tab` cycles the permission modes: `default` (asks before edits and commands) → `acceptEdits` → `plan` (read only) | | Stop it while it is working | `Ctrl+C` | | Approve a plan it has made | Choose **"Yes, manually approve edits"**, so it still asks before each change. Choose "No, keep planning" to change the plan first | | Start a new conversation, with nothing from the last one | `/clear` | | See the permission rules in force | `/permissions` | | See which model it is using, for your AI-use log | It is shown above the prompt; `/model` also opens a picker | | Leave | `/exit` | Use `default` mode unless a block says otherwise. When it asks to edit a file or run a command, read the request before you answer: approving without reading turns `default` into no protection at all. ## Framing and mental models This block sets out the ideas that the rest of the workshop builds on. There are no participant coding exercises; the block is presentation, short discussion, and a comprehension check. *⏱ ~15 minutes* Two words recur all day. An assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. is any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is an assistant that acts: it reads across your project, and, depending on its permission mode, edits files and runs commands. Claude Code and Posit Assistant are agents; a chat window that only answers is not. The pages use "assistant" when what they say applies to any tool, and "agent" when the tool is doing work on your files. ## What is a large language model? A large language model (LLM) is a statistical model trained to predict the next token (roughly, the next fragment of text) given the tokens before it. Modern LLMs are trained on a substantial portion of the public internet, including code repositories, technical documentation, and prose. Every tool in this workshop is built on LLMs. Claude Code uses Anthropic's Claude models. Posit Assistant runs on Posit AI or on the provider key you configure. GitHub Copilot offers several providers: Anthropic's Claude family, OpenAI's GPT family, and Google's Gemini family. Where a tool exposes a model picker, the choice matters, because models differ measurably in code quality, instruction-following, and propensity to hallucinate library calls or function signatures that do not exist. For the present workshop, you do not need to develop strong opinions about which model is best. You do need to know that the choice exists, that it changes the output, and that if a model produces consistently poor suggestions for your work and your plan lets you choose, switching is a cheap experiment. ## Two modes of execution An assistant can act on your behalf in two quite different modes. The first is synchronous and local: inline completion, Claude Code in your terminal and Posit Assistant in your IDE all work on your machine, respond in seconds, and can be interrupted at any point. This is the mode you use all day. Their scope is whatever the tool can reach: the current file for inline completion, the project folder and the output of the commands it runs for Claude Code, your live R session for Posit Assistant. The second is asynchronous and remote. An agent such as the Copilot cloud agent takes a task, works on its own branch on someone else's servers, and returns a pull request for you to review some minutes later. You meet it only in the *Going further* sections of Blocks 4, 6 and 9. The two modes invite different verification. The synchronous mode invites you to watch and interrupt; the asynchronous mode invites you to write a precise specification, walk away, and review what comes back. Block 4 refines this into a ladder of autonomy, from suggesting the next line to acting with no prompts (acting remotely is the extra rung in its *Going further* section), and Block 5 shows how much of the specification can be written once, in instructions and skills. ## Why the context window matters LLMs do not have memory between calls. Each interaction starts fresh, with whatever you supply as context. The context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window. is the upper limit on how much text the model can consider in a single call. This is the technical fact that motivates everything else in the workshop: instructions exist to inject persistent context into a system that has none; skills exist to make procedural context available on demand. And because instructions and skills are only context, which the model may or may not follow, Block 6 adds controls that hold whether or not the model reads them. If you remember nothing else from this block, remember that the AI sees only what you give it, and that everything it sees has left your machine. The rest of the workshop is mostly about giving it the right things, and checking what it does with them. ## Discussion Take three minutes. Think about the two questions below on your own, then post a short answer to each in the Zoom chat. The facilitator picks out the most interesting answers to discuss as a group. 1. What kinds of task would you not delegate to AI at all? 2. How do you use AI tools at the moment? Chat in the browser, IDE chats, terminal agents such as Claude Code? The discussion does not need to reach consensus. Its purpose is to surface the criteria participants already apply intuitively, which will inform how they use these tools after the workshop. ## Check your understanding **Which statement best describes the difference between a local agent such as Claude Code and an asynchronous cloud agent?**
**True or false: a large language model has no memory between calls, so each interaction starts with only the context you supply.** ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
agent An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.
AI-use log A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.
assistant Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.
characterisation test A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.
context window The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.
fresh R session An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work, such as the one Rscript starts. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
````` ::: :::
